paragraphs.text: Long-distance trade across the dry interior of Asia depended less on roads than on places to stop. A caravan of camels could cover perhaps thirty or forty kilometres in a day, and at the end of each stage its merchants needed water, shelter, fodder for the animals and some protection from thieves; a caravan could include hundreds of animals, and it moved at the pace of the slowest of them. Over many centuries, rulers, wealthy merchants and charitable foundations answered this need by building walled inns along the main routes. Known across much of the region as caravanserais, they were spaced roughly a day’s journey apart, and a traveller crossing Persia or Anatolia might sleep in a different one every night for weeks.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The typical caravanserai was built to a remarkably consistent plan. A single gate, large enough for a loaded camel and narrow enough to be closed quickly, opened onto a courtyard surrounded by rooms. Animals were kept in the courtyard or in stables along the outer walls, while merchants slept and stored their goods in raised chambers overlooking them, so that no one had to leave his bales out of sight. A well or cistern stood near the centre, and around it there was often a raised platform where travellers could sit and talk in the cool of the evening. The outer walls were thick and largely without windows, which kept the interior cool in summer and made the building easy to defend. In some regions the corners were strengthened with towers that made the inns resemble small forts.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The design varied with climate and terrain. In the mountains of the Caucasus and eastern Anatolia, where snow could close the passes for weeks, some caravanserais were covered entirely, the courtyard being replaced by a vaulted hall in which people and animals sheltered together around fires, the smoke escaping through openings in the roof, which also let in a little light. In the deserts of central Iran, by contrast, the courtyard was large and open, and builders gave particular attention to water, sometimes digging channels that brought it underground from distant hills. Inns in cities had a different character again. There they served as warehouses, offices and markets, and many survive today as bazaars or shopping arcades.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Archaeologists have found caravanserais surprisingly hard to date. Many were rebuilt several times on the same foundations, and an inscription over the gate often records only the most recent patron rather than the original builder. Pottery and coins found in the rooms show when a building was in use, but not when it was first constructed. Recent surveys have combined satellite images, which reveal the outlines of ruined walls invisible from the ground, with radiocarbon dating of charcoal found in hearths and mortar. The results suggest that the network was denser and older than written records imply, with some routes lined with inns several centuries before the first travellers described them, and some inns that appear on no map at all have been found this way.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Who paid for these buildings, and why, is another question the surveys have helped to answer. Some were plainly commercial ventures that charged travellers for a room and fodder. Many more appear to have been free, at least for a certain number of nights, because they were endowed by rulers or wealthy individuals as acts of public generosity. Such foundations were usually supported by the income from shops, farmland or mills set aside for the purpose. The documents that established them sometimes specify in detail how the building was to be maintained, how many guards were to be employed and how the well was to be kept clean. Neglect of these duties could, in principle, lead to the loss of the endowment.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: For merchants, the inns were more than places to sleep. Many had a resident keeper who knew the local roads, the state of the wells ahead and which stretches were unsafe. They were where prices were learned, partners found and letters exchanged, and where news from one end of a route could reach the other within weeks. Historians have argued that this exchange of information was as important to long-distance trade as the physical protection the buildings offered, since a merchant who knew what silk was fetching three cities away could decide where to sell before he arrived. Ideas, techniques and stories travelled the same way, and some scholars trace the spread of particular styles of decoration along the chain of inns on a single route.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The decline of the caravanserai was gradual. As sea routes carried a growing share of long-distance trade from the sixteenth century onwards, and later as railways and motor roads replaced the camel, the inns lost their purpose. Many were abandoned, quarried for stone or left to the desert. Others were absorbed into growing towns and can still be traced in the plan of the streets. In recent decades, however, a number have been restored, some as hotels or cultural centres, and several countries along the old routes have sought international recognition for their surviving examples. Critics note that restoration can erase the evidence archaeologists need, and that a caravanserai turned into a smart hotel tells visitors very little about the crowded, noisy and practical place it once was.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: A dictionary looks like the most authoritative of books. Its entries are brief and confident, its definitions admit no doubt, and generations of readers have settled arguments by consulting it, though few of them ever ask who wrote the entries they rely on. Yet the confidence is partly an effect of the format. Behind every entry lies a long chain of decisions about which words to include, which meanings to list first and how to describe words whose use is still changing. Most of those decisions are made by people who would be the first to say that the language does not belong to them. The authority, in other words, is borrowed from the format rather than claimed by the authors.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The earliest dictionaries in many European languages were not attempts to record the whole language at all. They were lists of difficult words, often borrowed from Latin or Greek, explained for readers who had not had a classical education. Ordinary words such as ’hand’ or ’go’ were left out because everyone was assumed to know them. The explanations were often short, and sometimes little more than a single synonym. It was only from the eighteenth century that lexicographers began to aim at completeness, and with that ambition came a new problem: once every word is to be included, someone must decide what counts as a word of the language and what is merely slang, dialect or error, a question that has never been fully settled.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: For a long time the answer was to rely on the usage of respected writers. An entry would be supported by quotations from literature, and a word or meaning found only in speech or in popular writing might be marked as vulgar or omitted entirely. Spelling, too, was fixed in this period, often by choosing one of several forms that were then in use. This approach gave the dictionary a moral as well as a practical role, since its compilers saw themselves as guardians of good usage against decline. Some openly hoped that their work would fix the language in its best state and prevent further change, a hope that the history of every living language has since disappointed.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The great historical dictionaries of the nineteenth century took a different view. Their editors set out to describe how each word had actually been used over time, and to do so they needed evidence on an enormous scale. They appealed to the public for help, and thousands of volunteers read books and sent in slips of paper, each recording a single use of a word together with its source and date. Some volunteers sent in tens of thousands of slips over many years, and a few became experts in particular periods or fields. The slips were sorted by word and then by meaning, and editors wrote definitions only after examining all of them. One such project collected several million slips and took more than seventy years to complete, by which time its earliest volumes were already out of date.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Today the slips have been replaced by corpora, collections of text stored electronically and running to billions of words drawn from newspapers, books, websites and transcribed conversation. The largest of them are updated continuously as new material is published. A lexicographer can now see in seconds every recorded use of a word, how often it appears and which words tend to surround it, so that patterns that no single reader could notice become visible at once. This has changed not only the speed of the work but its results. Corpus evidence showed, for example, that the most frequent meaning of many common words was not the one dictionaries had traditionally placed first, and entries were reordered accordingly. Corpora also revealed words and phrases that were common in speech but had never been recorded in any dictionary.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The same evidence has made it harder for dictionaries to act as judges. When a disputed usage appears millions of times in careful, edited writing, it is difficult to go on calling it a mistake, and most modern dictionaries now describe how words are used and leave readers to decide which usages to adopt. They still offer guidance, typically in short notes warning that a particular use may be criticised by some readers, but they no longer claim the authority to rule. Not everyone welcomes this shift. Teachers and editors in particular sometimes complain that a dictionary which records everything helps no one to choose. Others argue that the choice was never really the dictionary’s to make.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The newest challenge is the pace of change itself. New words and meanings now spread across the world in weeks, and online dictionaries can add them almost as quickly, with updates published every few months rather than in a new edition every decade. Lexicographers must decide whether a word has become established or is merely a passing fashion. Many new words disappear within a year or two, and a dictionary that includes them too quickly soon looks dated. Lexicographers therefore generally wait until it has appeared over a period of time in a range of independent sources. The dictionary, in other words, still follows the language rather than leading it, however quickly it now moves.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The age at which children begin formal schooling varies more than most parents realise. In some countries children start at four, in many at six, and in several northern European countries not until seven. Each system has its defenders, and each can point to children who thrive under it. Parents, meanwhile, often choose a school long before they have any idea which system suits their own child. What has changed in recent years is the volume of evidence, and with it a growing argument that many countries start formal lessons too early, pushing reading and arithmetic onto children who would learn them more easily a year or two later. The evidence is not all on one side, however, and much of it has been read selectively.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The argument for an early start is partly practical and partly about fairness. Parents need childcare, and a free school place from the age of four relieves many families of a considerable cost. For single parents in particular, the difference can decide whether they are able to work at all. The economist Laura Chen points out that children from poorer homes often arrive at school with smaller vocabularies than their classmates, and that an early start gives schools more time to close that gap before it widens. In her analysis, delaying school would benefit mainly those children whose homes already provide the kind of stimulation that school offers. Her figures come mainly from countries where most children already start school at four or five.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: I find this argument persuasive as far as it goes, but it depends on what the early years of school actually contain. Chen’s case is really an argument for early education, not for early formal instruction, and the two are not the same. The psychologist Tomas Berg, who has compared classrooms in several countries, notes that children who spend their first years in play-based settings, where language is developed through talk, stories and games rather than worksheets, show no lasting disadvantage in reading by the age of eleven. This holds even where formal reading lessons began two years later than elsewhere. Berg is careful to add that his comparison cannot separate the effect of the starting age from other differences between the countries.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: There is also evidence that the youngest children in a class are at a disadvantage wherever the starting age is set. Because most systems admit all children born within a single year, a child born just before the cut-off date may be almost twelve months younger than the oldest classmate. Studies in many countries have found that these youngest children are more likely to be placed in lower groups, less likely to be selected for sports teams and, in some countries, more likely to be referred for extra learning support. The effect is strongest in the first years of school and fades later, but it does not always disappear. Sara Okafor, who has studied this effect, argues that what matters is not a child’s absolute age so much as his or her age relative to the rest of the class. Some parents have responded by timing births, where they can, to avoid the end of the school year.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: If that is right, simply raising the starting age for everyone would not solve the problem, since some child would always be the youngest. Okafor’s own proposal is more modest: allow the parents of the youngest children to delay entry by a year without penalty, and adjust test scores for age whenever children are compared. Some school systems already do both. Critics reply that flexible entry tends to be used most by well-informed, wealthier families, and that it could therefore widen the very gaps that an early start was meant to reduce, although the same objection could be made to almost any policy that depends on parents’ choices.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Much of the public debate assumes that a later start means a longer wait at home. It need not: children in those countries are not simply at home until their seventh birthday. In the countries where formal school begins at seven, almost all children attend kindergarten for several years beforehand, and these settings are publicly funded and closely regulated. The historian Anton Weiss has shown that the late starting age in those countries grew out of a long tradition of kindergarten education rather than from any decision to keep young children away from learning. Copying the starting age without copying that tradition, he warns, would give children the worst of both systems.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: My conclusion is that the question as usually posed, whether children should start school at four or at seven, is the wrong one, because it invites a simple answer to a question that does not have one. What matters more is what children are asked to do when they arrive. An early start in a setting that values play, conversation and curiosity seems to do no harm and may well help children from poorer homes, while an early start devoted to formal tests and worksheets offers little that could not be learned more easily later. The label on the building matters far less than the activity inside it. Countries that change the age without changing the classroom are unlikely to notice much difference.
paragraphs.label: G

explanation.ru: «left out because everyone was assumed to know them» → A.

explanation.ru: Слово из устной речи «might be marked as vulgar or omitted» → B. F — ловушка: они надеялись остановить изменения, но надежда не оправдалась.

items.quote: entries were reordered accordingly
items.prompt: Evidence from electronic text collections

explanation.en: Corpus evidence showed the commonest meaning was not first, so “entries were reordered accordingly” → C.

explanation.ru: Корпус показал, что самое частое значение не стояло первым, и «entries were reordered accordingly» → C.

items.prompt: Adults who started school at seven go on to earn more than those who started earlier.

items.quote: Chen’s case is really an argument for early education, not for early formal instruction
items.prompt: Chen’s evidence supports early learning rather than early formal teaching.

explanation.ru: «Chen’s case is really an argument for early education, not for early formal instruction» → YES.

items.quote: less likely to be selected for sports teams
items.prompt: The youngest pupils in a class are more often picked for school sports teams.

explanation.en: “less likely to be selected for sports teams” → NO. The “more likely” in that sentence refers to lower groups and support.
explanation.kk: «less likely to be selected for sports teams» → NO. Сол сөйлемдегі «more likely» төменгі топ пен қосымша көмекке қатысты.
explanation.ru: «less likely to be selected for sports teams» → NO. В том же предложении есть «more likely» — но про нижние группы и дополнительную поддержку.

items.quote: and that it could therefore widen the very gaps that an early start was meant to reduce
items.prompt: Flexible entry has already been shown to widen the gap between richer and poorer families.

explanation.en: Critics say flexible entry “could” widen gaps — a fear, not a demonstrated result, and the writer does not judge it → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Сыншылар икемді қабылдау алшақтықты «could» ұлғайтуы мүмкін дейді — бұл дәлелденген дерек емес, қауіп қана; автор баға бермейді → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Критики говорят, что гибкий приём «could» увеличить разрыв, — это опасение, а не доказанный факт; сам автор это не оценивает → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: these settings are publicly funded and closely regulated

explanation.ru: «these settings are publicly funded» → NO. Об оплате сказано прямо, поэтому это не NOT GIVEN.
